https://www.pocketgamer.com/sofie-scout-.text: Features I happily paid to support Sofie Scout despite my terrible endless running skills Scout's honour By Catherine Dellosa | Jul 23 iOS + Android | Sofie Scout - Road to Poland Prefer Pocket Gamer on Google I've never really experienced what it's like to miss the bus, as I'm usually a pretty prompt pupil, but I can imagine how stressful it must be - especially if you're heading to a once-in-a-lifetime event. That's exactly what the World Scout Jamboree is for poor lil Sofie, and given how I too was once a scout myself, I know that the struggle is very, very real. Now, while I personally wouldn't sprint on foot across Europe just to get to the said jamboree, I admire Sofie's unstoppable determination in Sofie Scout , which is why I have sworn to do everything I can to help her reach Gdansk, Poland in one piece - even if that means leaping across dangerous ravines that seem to appear out of nowhere and vaulting over wayward chickens just randomly clucking away in the middle of the road. Because that is, essentially, what this side-scrolling endless runner is all about. You have one button to jump and another to slide across the floor, as Sofie automatically dashes across the screen filled with all sorts of randomised obstacles. Memorisation will get you nowhere here, as while one run might have you hopping over a cow and then landing on your face, another run might throw an ancient totem at you to cut your trip short. This is where things can get incredibly challenging, because while the premise sounds absolutely charming, you shouldn't make the mistake of thinking it's all easy-peasy from here. The difficulty level is totally S-tier, because you'll need to contend with everything from fiddly jumps that need to be perfectly timed, to tripping just because the tip of your foot grazed a platform you're supposed to jump over by a mere millimetre. I do wish there was some kind of checkpoint that'll keep me from starting over from scratch every time I fall, but thankfully, the absolutely gorgeous pixel art in the background keeps the frustrations at bay. That said, sometimes, it's also a challenge to figure out which items are just background fodder and which ones are actual bushes I need to leap over in the foreground, but hey - nobody said running cross-country on foot would be easy. In any case, I did purchase this endless runner out of pocket simply because I wanted to help support IRL scouts Juno and Ellie make enough money to attend the World Scout Jamboree. Their £3,600 goal, I would assume, is no easy feat, so if my $2.99 can help even just a tiny bit, I'm happy to do my part. If Juno and Ellie's quest sounds at all interesting to you, might I suggest giving Sofie Scout - Road to Poland a go? If nothing else, you'll get to test your own resilience, patience, and quick reflexes across a cute pixel-art runner - and who knows? You might even make it to Poland yourself. Do let me know how it goes, though, as I've never made it past 100 kilometres at this point. This is what happens when I don't keep up with my cardio… Download now! Sofie Scout - Road to Poland Catherine Dellosa Catherine plays video games for a living and writes because she’s in love with words. Her Young Adult contemporary novel, For The Win: The Not-So-Epic Quest Of A Non-Playable Character, is her third book published by Penguin Random House SEA - a poignant love letter to gamer geeks, mythological creatures, teenage heartbreak, and everything in between. She one day hopes to soar the skies as a superhero, but for now, she strongly believes in saving lives through her works in fiction. Check out her books at bit.ly/catherinedellosabooks, or follow her on FB/IG/Twitter at @thenoobwife. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clye.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, AndrÃ¡s Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg By Nick Thorpe in Hungary Published 22 minutes ago Hungary's parliament has elected AndrÃ¡s Baka, 73, a respected judge and former head of the Supreme Court, as head of state. The Hungarian president is a largely figurehead role, but Baka's rule promises to be tempestuous. His task will be to monitor Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar's efforts to dismantle the interlocking economic and political powerhouse established by former Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n. He will also oversee the writing of a new constitution, to replace OrbÃ¡n's constitution of 2011. "We cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," AndrÃ¡s Baka told Parliament, after he was elected by 140 votes to 6. "The majority of society now feels a sense of liberation and hope. Others feel disappointment and uncertainty," he said. "In a democratic society, this is not an anomaly, but a natural state of affairs." All 51 MPs belonging to OrbÃ¡n's party Fidesz walked out of the chamber before the vote, in protest against the ousting of their favourite, TamÃ¡s Sulyok, from the post last month . In his speech, AndrÃ¡s Baka promised the broadest possible debate on the creation of a new constitution. Since taking office in early May, the new Magyar government has lost no time attacking OrbÃ¡n's legacy. Twenty-seven laws have been passed, and two amendments to the constitution. The states of emergency - migrants, Covid, and war in Ukraine - which OrbÃ¡n used to govern by decree, were all cancelled. The Sovereignty Protection Office, which the Fidesz government used to attack critical journalists and NGOs, was abolished, and an National Asset Recovery and Protection Office was established, with sweeping powers to investigate and prosecute individuals accused of stealing state funds under the former government. Fidesz accuses the Tisza government of establishing a "tyranny". Ironically, they removed Baka from his post as president of the Supreme Court in 2011, for attempting to stop them undermine the rule of law. Public service radio and TV have been off air since 9 July , as news programmes are revamped. The stated aim is to restore their independence, from their Fidesz-era role as government propaganda organs. Other key changes came under Amendments 16 and 17 of the constitution, limiting the prime minister to two terms in office, and MPs to three. The ability of the Constitutional Court to oversee acts of parliament, taken away by Fidesz, was also restored. If the Tisza majority expects Baka to be a tame president, they may get a rude awakening. In a BBC interview before he was asked to take the post, he made clear he opposes the limitation of MPs' terms as an intrusion on the right of voters to freely choose their representatives. Baka served for 17 years as the Hungarian judge at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. "I am not a political man," he told the BBC last month. "I got involved in politics through my professional, legal way of thinking." Baka was elected today as a transitional figure. Under the constitutional amendment which made his presidency possible, the new president will likely only be in place until the new constitution comes into force - or for maximum of five years. Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Baka made it clear that he intended to push back against the Hungarian tendency to trust in powerful leaders. "The state is not there for itself," he said, at the end of his speech. "It is there for the people." Related topics Hungary More on this story What does new Hungarian PM PÃ©ter Magyar stand for? An Auckland jury has found former Kelston Boys’ High School teacher and published author Murray Sakey guilty of sexually abusing two boys. During the trial, the retiree accepted he was attracted to children, had undertaken shirtless photo shoots with one of the victims and slept in a bed with both boys, but denied ever sexually abusing them. The jury of 11 men and one woman were not convinced. Sakey, now in his mid 70s, was found guilty last week in the Auckland District Court of seven indecency charges, but was acquitted of one count of threatening to kill. Up until Friday, Sakey had interim name suppression in relation to the abuse. It meant the Herald was unable to report his identity or reveal that he was convicted of possessing child exploitation material in 2024. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. The Herald ’s reporting on Sakey’s earlier offending prompted the two complainants in the latest case to come forward, alleging Sakey had been sexually abusive to them over three decades ago. One of the victims told police in 2024 he had earlier believed Sakey would go to the grave without facing accountability. “I never thought this day would come around,” he said to the interviewing officer. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Murray Sakey previously pleaded guilty to having hundreds of child exploitation images. Sakey was sentenced in May 2024 in the Waitākere District Court. Photo / Katie Harris “As soon as I realised and found out that he’d been found with objectionable material and written whatever he’s f***ing written, I said, ‘Okay that’s good enough for me’, and I rang up and initialised talking to someone [from police].” At the time of the sexual abuse, the music teacher lived in West Auckland and held music practices at his home with children, some from Kelston Boys’ High School. For one of the boys he was found guilty of abusing, Sakey saw himself as a “father figure” and admitted to sleeping in a bed with him more than a handful of times. “[In] lots of places in Europe it happens all the time, I didn’t consider it inappropriate,” he said when police questioned him about the sleeping arrangement. In the same 2024 interview where the abuse allegations were levelled at him, Sakey told the investigating officer he found children attractive. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “Police have an idea [that] you can’t find the look of a child attractive … It seems the police have no idea what beauty is.” While he claimed the attraction was not sexual, he said: “Any child is attractive.” Sakey even said the interviewing officer herself had the “shape I like in women”. The complainants The victims crossed paths as children but were not known to each other when they reported the abuse separately three decades later. The first victim to testify in court said in a video interview that he largely grew up without a father and Sakey “almost became that kind of a figure”. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. He pointed to two occasions when he woke up to Sakey sexually abusing him. The man said he was haunted by not speaking up about the abuse when questioned by a concerned relative years ago. “It’s something I can never take back.” Sakey would host youth band practices at his home and was heavily involved in the music community. The jury heard he had set Google Calendar reminders in recent years to tell Sakey’s family about the abuse he endured, but kept putting the disclosure off. Then he saw the 2024 article about the child exploitation material and it “brought it all home”. While he had kept the abuse close to his chest for three decades, he said during a police interview he may have told one of his close childhood friends. Though the pair hadn’t spoken in many years, and unbeknown to the complainant, his childhood friend would appear for the prosecution on the second day of Sakey’s trial. The childhood friend told the court he learned what his old mate had endured about 30 years ago. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “He seemed upset about it and [was] probably wanting to confide in somebody who would listen. “He told me that in confidence, so I’d never repeat it to anybody else.” The witness said “everyone” at Kelston Boys’ High School had an opinion about Sakey and what he was like. “There was lots of inappropriate behaviour but nothing that anyone else sort of raised alarm bells on.” Auckland man Murray Sakey at his earlier court case. Photo / Katie Harris Sakey repeatedly painted the second victim as a liar and untrustworthy. That man first reported the sexual abuse to police in 2002, but the case was not progressed. A summary of his 2002 complaint included claims the former teacher abused him in the shower, in bed and took naked images of him using a sheet over a ranch slider as a backdrop. These allegations were consistent with the abuse report he made in 2024. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. His criminal history of largely theft and driving-related offending was brought to the jury’s attention, including giving police the wrong name after he was pulled over. When questioned about the incident by the defence, the victim said he was a street kid with a past, and it wasn’t the “crime of the century”. “You’re trying to discredit me with one incident? “Making out that one instance and I’m a liar forever.” Defence lawyer Caitlin Oxnam asked whether the complainant had concocted allegations about Sakey to get a financial payout, as the ex-teacher claimed. The victim denied the accusation. “I’ve got nothing to lie about … I don’t have to come here and tell a story, it’s the truth. “I’ve unequivocally told the truth to this court.” Advertisement Advertise with NZME. The author and the child abuse material In May 2024, Sakey was sentenced to five months’ home detention and 15 months’ intensive supervision after pleading guilty to three charges of possessing objectionable publications . This offending was discovered after the new occupants of a home found his USB drive containing 490 images and a Word document with a “graphic narrative-type story” on it. Police subsequently found 109 other objectionable images on Sakey’s devices. The prosecution said the offending occurred over a 12-year period. Sakey claimed he was using the content as “inspiration” for his book writing. He publishes fiction books under a pseudonym. One of the books Murray Sakey wrote under a pseudonym. Photo / File The “teen adult fiction” books he’d written featured illustrations or photos of pre-adolescent boys on their covers, some styled as angels. The novels range from fantasy to mystery. One, titled Prague: An Unforgettable Story of Betrayal and Redemption, features an 11-year-old caught up in “a major child prostitution operation across Europe”. While under cross-examination during last week’s trial for child sexual abuse, prosecutor Clare Antenen brought up his earlier online offending. She asked Sakey how the objectionable material, including the Word document with sexual stories involving children, ended up on his devices. Sakey again claimed he downloaded the material to inspire his own story writing. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “I didn’t read them right through; they weren’t what I needed for my writing.” He claimed that when he realised the stories he had downloaded were of child sexual abuse, he had a feeling of “revulsion”. “Why didn’t you delete it, get rid of it, destroy it?” Antenen responded. Sakey said he “put it aside and forgot about it”. “A normal reaction would have been to delete it as soon as you saw it,” Antenen said. “Possibly,” he replied. The verdict Just hours after Judge Terence Singh sent the jury out to deliberate on the eighth day of trial, a decision was reached. Guilty, on all but one of the eight charges. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Sakey was taken into custody after the verdict, ahead of a hearing on Friday to determine name suppression and bail. During that hearing, Oxnam told the court Sakey was no longer seeking suppression and would make no further bail submissions. The Crown’s position was that Sakey should remain in custody. Judge Singh remanded Sakey in custody until sentencing. Sakey’s interim suppression lapsed after the hearing. Katie Harris is an Auckland-based journalist who covers issues such as sexual assault, workplace misconduct, media, crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2020.
